content: Write a cover letter for a junior software developer position.

# Cover Letter — Junior Software Developer

**[Your Name]**
[City, State] | [Phone] | [Email] | [GitHub/Portfolio URL] | [LinkedIn]

[Date]

**[Hiring Manager Name]**
[Company Name]
[Company Address or "City, State"]

Dear [Hiring Manager Name / Hiring Team],

I'm writing to apply for the Junior Software Developer position at [Company Name], which I found on [job board / company careers page / referral source]. As a [recent computer science graduate / self-taught developer / bootcamp graduate] with hands-on experience building [web applications / APIs / mobile apps] in [primary language or stack], I'm excited by the opportunity to contribute to a team working on [specific product, mission, or technology the company is known for].

In my most recent role as [internship title / project or role] at [Company/School/Project], I [built or contributed to a specific thing]. For example, I developed [brief project description — e.g., "a REST API in Node.js and PostgreSQL that handled inventory data for 500+ product SKUs"], which [measurable or concrete outcome — e.g., "reduced manual data entry time by roughly 40%"]. That project taught me how to [relevant skill: write testable code, work with Git in a team, debug under a deadline, translate vague requirements into tickets].

I'm particularly drawn to [Company Name] because [specific, genuine reason — their open-source work, a product you use, their engineering blog, their approach to mentorship]. I noticed [specific detail], and it aligns closely with the kind of work I want to grow into. I'm also comfortable being early in my career: I ask questions, I take code review seriously, and I ramp up quickly on new tools — I picked up [technology] in [timeframe] to complete [project].

My core technical skills include [Language 1, Language 2], [Framework], [Database], and [Git/Docker/AWS/testing framework]. You can see examples of my work at [GitHub or portfolio link], including [name of your best project].

I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I can support the team at [Company Name]. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
**[Your Name]**

---

## Tips for customizing this

- **Replace vague claims with specifics.** "Built a full-stack app" is weaker than "built a Django app that lets users track workouts, with 200 lines of unit tests and CI via GitHub Actions."
- **Mirror the job posting's language.** If they say "React and TypeScript," those exact words should appear if they're true for you.
- **Keep it to one page** — roughly 250–400 words. Hiring managers skim.
- **Address a real person** when you can. Check LinkedIn or the company's team page; "Dear Hiring Team" is fine as a fallback, but avoid "To Whom It May Concern."
- **Lead with enthusiasm for their work, not just your need for a job.** One sentence proving you researched the company beats three paragraphs about yourself.
- **Don't apologize for inexperience.** Skip phrases like "although I lack professional experience." Frame what you *have* done instead.

Want me to tailor this to a specific job posting or your actual background? Paste the listing and a few details about your projects and I'll draft a version you can send as-is.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

# Cover Letter — Junior Software Developer
*Version for a reader who already knows you*

I've written this for the case where the reader has context on you already — a manager you interned under, someone you met at a meetup, a team you contracted with, or an internal transfer. The main shift: no self-introduction, no credential recap, no explaining what the company does. Straight to the ask, the new information, and the fit.

---

**[Your Name]** | [Phone] | [Email] | [GitHub]

[Date]

Hi [Name],

I saw the Junior Software Developer opening on [team name] and wanted to throw my hat in before the posting closes on [date] — I've applied through [system], but wanted to reach out directly.

Since we last worked together on [project], I've been [what changed: finishing the CS degree / shipping X at Y / going deep on Z]. The most relevant piece: [one specific thing that's new since they last saw you — "I rebuilt the reporting pipeline in Go, which cut the nightly job from 40 minutes to 6," or "I've been maintaining a Rails service in production, including on-call"]. That's the gap I knew I had when we talked in [month], and it's closed.

What draws me to this role specifically is [concrete detail about the team's work — the migration they're doing, the product surface, the fact that it's the same codebase you touched]. I already know [the codebase / the deploy process / how the team works], so I'd expect to be useful in weeks rather than months.

You know how I work, so I won't oversell it. If it's helpful, I'm happy to talk through [specific thing you'd want to discuss: scope, the team's current priorities, where they need coverage]. And if I'm not the right shape for this one, I'd genuinely appreciate a straight answer on that — it's useful information either way.

Thanks, [Name].

[Your Name]

---

## What changed and why

| First version | This version |
|---|---|
| Formal salutation, full address block | First name, minimal header |
| Explains who you are and what you've built | Assumes they know; reports only what's *new* |
| Justifies interest in the company | Names a specific team detail instead |
| Lists tech stack | Cut entirely — they've seen your work |
| ~350 words | ~200 words |

**A few notes on the tone:** the line "You know how I work, so I won't oversell it" is doing real work — it signals you understand the relationship and aren't wasting their time with a performance. Cut it if the relationship is more distant than warm.

Two sub-cases that shift things further:

- **Internal transfer.** Add one sentence on transition logistics ("I've spoken with [current manager] about timing") — internal readers care about that more than your skills.
- **Referral, where the reader knows *of* you but hasn't worked with you.** Name the referrer in the first line, and restore one sentence of concrete evidence, since secondhand knowledge is thinner than they'd like.

Send me the actual relationship and the posting and I'll sharpen this to something you can send today.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

# Cover Letter — Junior Software Developer
*Short version, for a reader who knows you*

Hi [Name],

I'm applying for the Junior Software Developer role on [team] — I'd like the job, and I think I'm ready for it now in a way I wasn't when we last talked.

The change since [project]: [one specific thing — "I rebuilt the reporting pipeline in Go and cut the nightly job from 40 minutes to 6"]. That was the gap, and it's closed.

I already know [the codebase / the deploy process / how the team works], so ramp-up should be short. Happy to talk through [scope / timing / where you need coverage] whenever it's useful.

Thanks, [Name].

[Your Name]

---

**What moved:** the ask is now sentence one instead of paragraph one, and everything that explained *why this company* is gone — a reader who knows you doesn't need it. Cut the credential list, the soft closing, and the "if I'm not right for this" line, which reads as hedging at this length.

**Placement notes:** this fits an email body, a LinkedIn message, or a Slack DM. If it's going in an application field that also takes a resume, keep the header line with your contact info. If it's a DM, drop the sign-off entirely.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

# Cover Letter — Junior Software Developer
*Short version, for a reader who knows you*

Hi [Name],

I'm applying for the Junior Software Developer role on [team] — I'd like the job, and I think I'm ready for it now in a way I wasn't when we last talked.

The change since [project]: [one specific thing — "I rebuilt the reporting pipeline in Go"]. That was the gap, and it's closed.

I already know [the codebase / the deploy process / how the team works], so ramp-up should be short. Happy to talk through [scope / timing / where you need coverage] whenever it's useful.

Thanks, [Name].

[Your Name]

---

**What changed:** only the outcome metric came out of the example placeholder. The sentence now names the work without quantifying its effect. Everything else is untouched.

**One thing to watch:** that metric was carrying most of the weight in the middle paragraph. Without it, "that was the gap, and it's closed" is doing the persuading on its own. If you can't cite results, the next strongest substitute is scope or duration rather than impact — "I've been maintaining it in production since [month]," or "I owned that service end to end." Both describe the work without claiming a measured outcome. Say the word if you want a version built that way.
